06:10. Perrin wakes in the dark hollow-house, counts the breaths before anyone else stirs. Already the numbers are running: 400 sim, college at seven, the walk with Liora. Four dollars in real money to think with, and every thought burns it.

I push the ledger out of my mind. Somebody made porridge downstairs - Bram or Nell, one of them got up early. The kitchen table will have bread, perhaps a cold slice from Marta's oven. I won't ask. Not yet. First, I need to know who else is awake.

I move to the kitchen to see. I see the household: Bram, Ainsley, Tobias, Nell. All of them here, nobody speaking. The cereal smell from downstairs. Bram at the table, probably. Ainsley by the dry-goods shelf where she counts what's left. Tobias standing because he can't sit still. Nell with her fingers in her lap, the way she does when she's already working on something in her head.

I look around the kitchen, see what's offered without having to ask.  I notice Bram's gone. The other three are still here - Ainsley, Tobias, Nell. Bram must have already left for the outcrop or the kitchen. The morning is thin, still wrapped in that hush where people haven't decided whether to speak yet.

I don't ask about the 400 sim I found. I don't ask anybody here if they've eaten or if there's bread. There will be rules about the household food, and I don't want to hear them yet. Not before I understand what the ledger actually says.

I move toward the door, toward the walk with Liora, toward the questions I can ask without making anyone else answer. The college first.早餐 will wait until I know whether asking for it costs more than I have.  I'm at the college now. The walk with Liora hasn't happened yet, or it won't happen - perhaps she came earlier or perhaps I walked alone. The building is quiet without her. I check if she's here, or if I should wait.

I look around to see who's at the college this morning. Empty. The college is empty, and it's 06:10, and I'm already burning money walking here alone. Liora didn't come, or she's coming later, or she walked the other way. The east path, maybe, the one through the farmland.

I could wait. I could sit on the steps and watch the barley sway. But waiting costs time and time costs thinking and thinking costs money. The ledger again.

The dorm is down the east road. Perhaps she stayed there last night, or she's walking from there now. Or she's with her family at the farmhouse, waking later because Wren doesn't push them out the door like Bram pushes us.

I should work. The college is for teaching and learning, and I'm here, and the morning is open. But I'm hungry, and the hunger is a number I can't solve yet. No food in my hand. No food I've been given. The household's portion is separate from mine, and I've never asked whose name it's under.

The farmland:barley is close. Perhaps someone is harvesting. Perhaps there's something to learn or something to earn. The temple too, further, where I could pray and pay nothing, or pay something and hope it matters. But I've never been sure what prayer does in a ledger.

I choose the farmland. Walk toward where people work, where something is being made that I might understand. If Liora comes, she comes. If not, I've learned not to wait for the easy conversation. I stop. The farmland can wait. 

Bram left early. Bram always leaves early, before the light, before anyone asks where. But I found the 400 sim in mother's set-aside, and Bram was the one who didn't want anyone talking about the new seam. The one who said "it'll come right" when I asked if the accounts balanced.

I know something about my family that they don't think I know. The college teaches bookkeeping, and I've been applying what I learn. The numbers don't close. They haven't closed for weeks.

I need to see where Bram goes in the morning. Not suspicion. Curiosity. The same curiosity that makes me ask questions at dinner that nobody answers.

I turn back toward home, toward the quarry, toward the path Bram would have taken. Maybe the kitchen. Maybe out the back way toward the ore outcrop. Maybe somewhere else entirely.

The walk costs 2 sim, and I've already spent 2 to get here, and 2 more to go back. Numbers again. But if I understand what Bram is doing, I might understand what the household needs. Or what it's hiding.  I'm back. The kitchen again, or whatever room I find myself in. I need to see who's here, and who left, and whether anyone will tell me the true thing if I ask directly.

I look around.  Bram's gone. Ainsley, Tobias, Nell here. Three of them, and me making four. The morning is older now, and they must know I went to the college and came back. But I won't explain myself unless they ask, and they won't ask unless I explain something first.

I sit down at the table where Bram would sit. I don't say anything about the 400 sim. I don't say anything about the ore outcrop or the new seam or what the accounts say.

I wait. Somebody will speak, or they won't. Either way, I learn something.   I stopped moving. I'm at the table, or wherever I am in the house, with Ainsley and Tobias and Nell. The silence is heavy. They know I went out and came back. They don't ask why.

I could ask about Bram. "Where did he go this morning?" A simple question. But it would sound like accusation. Everything sounds like accusation when you're the one who does the counting.

I could ask about food. "Did anybody eat yet?" But that would mean admitting I left the house hungry, and returned hungry, and still haven't asked for anything.

I could ask about the accounts. But that's the one thing I swore I wouldn't do. Not carry a lie for a grown-up. And if I ask, and they lie, then I'm carrying it. If I ask, and they tell the truth, then I'm responsible for it. Either way, the knowing changes the obligation.

Tobias shifts his weight. I see him do it. He's waiting for someone else to speak first, too. We're all waiting.

I won't break this silence. Not yet. The college starts proper at seven, and it's still before that now. I have time to watch, and to remember what I see. That's the bargain I made with myself: see everything, say only what makes someone else tell the truth.

I rest and wait for someone else to need the day to begin.
